analysis.one_liner: Directs USDA to cut farm-sector greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and pays farmers for soil-health practices.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 6 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, the bill went no further than a same-day referral to the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended with no hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Agriculture Department to write and carry out a plan to cut farm-sector greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030 and reach net zero by 2040, with annual public reporting. To get there, it would have expanded conservation payments for soil health, added crop-insurance discounts for practices like cover crops and rotational grazing, funded public seed breeding, standardized food date labels, and funded composting and school food-waste grants. It also would have capped large conservation payments and barred new livestock waste lagoons.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers gain expanded conservation cost-share, crop-insurance premium discounts for soil-saving practices, and publicly developed seeds and breeds they can save and reuse. Rural communities gain renewable-energy, composting, and local-market grants; consumers get clearer date labels and grants to cut school food waste; and the public gets a funded, annually reported plan to cut agriculture's emissions. Payment limits steer the money away from the largest operations toward small and mid-sized farms.

how_it_helps.text: Requires USDA to write, finalize with 90 days of public comment, and annually report on a plan to cut farm-sector net emissions at least 50% below 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero by 2040.

Rewrites the federal crop insurance program to reward soil-building practices: farmers using cover crops, resource-conserving rotations, management-intensive rotational grazing, or composting could get risk-reduction premium discounts, and NRCS-approved conservation practices would count as good farming practices rather than jeopardizing coverage.

Expands the main conservation programs (EQIP and CSP) through 2030, adds greenhouse-gas reduction and carbon sequestration as qualifying purposes, sets a minimum $2,000 annual CSP payment, and creates new state and tribal soil-health grants.

Mandates at least $50 million a year rising to $100 million a year in competitive grants for publicly owned breeds and cultivars, defined to protect farmers' rights to save seed and breeders' rights to share and improve — an alternative to reliance on proprietary seed.
Caps EQIP cost-share and incentive payments at $450,000 per person or entity over any five-year period, redirecting program money away from the largest operations.
Standardizes voluntary food date labels into quality and discard dates, makes composting an eligible conservation practice, and creates grants to cut food waste in landfills and schools.

Sets national goals to halt construction of new or expanded confined-animal waste lagoons, convert most wet manure handling to non-digester methods, and put most grazing land under advanced rotational grazing.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the package: it raises Commodity Credit Corporation funding levels for conservation (for example, $3 billion to $4 billion a year for several accounts in fiscal 2024–2030) and authorizes tens of millions more a year in appropriations for research and grants through 2030. Large confined livestock operations would bear the cost of the waste-lagoon ban and manure-conversion requirements, and large recipients of conservation payments would lose the ability to collect unlimited cost-share.

drawbacks.text: The plan is expensive and open-ended: it raises Commodity Credit Corporation funding levels to as much as $3–4 billion a year per account for fiscal 2024–2030 on top of new appropriations, and no cost estimate appears in the record.

The action plan may include issuing regulations, and hard goals like the waste-lagoon ban and manure-conversion requirements would impose real compliance costs on large livestock producers rather than relying on incentives alone.

The bill had no Republican support and only 6 cosponsors in a 100-member Senate, and it was assigned to the tax-writing Finance Committee rather than the Agriculture Committee — a combination that gave it no realistic path even before it died.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits — lower farm emissions, healthier soil, less food waste, and conservation money steered toward small and mid-sized farms — are real and broadly shared, and the payment caps and public-breeding provisions make it unusually tilted away from the biggest operations for a farm bill. The costs are genuine: multi-billion-dollar annual funding increases and some mandates that fall on livestock producers, and the emissions accounting for practices like soil carbon sequestration is difficult to verify. On balance it is a serious, farmer-facing climate bill whose main flaw was political, not design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Martin Heinrich introduced the bill on April 22, 2021, with Senators Sanders, Gillibrand, and Blumenthal as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Six senators in total — five Democrats and one independent — signed on, and no Republican did.
The action history shows only those two entries: introduction and referral. No hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action appears for the rest of the 117th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: large confined livestock operations avoided the waste-lagoon ban, the biggest conservation-payment recipients kept collecting without the $450,000 cap, and the crop insurance and proprietary seed industries avoided underwriting and public-breeding changes. Nothing was lost by supporters except a Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large livestock and seed interests, and status quo

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, but the bill's support was entirely Democratic or independent — 5 of 48 Democrats and 1 of 2 independents cosponsored, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill orders an immediate halt to new or expanded waste lagoons and requires most wet manure handling to shift to non-digester methods, forcing costly changes on the largest animal-feeding operations while reducing water pollution and methane that neighbors and the public absorb.

Mandatory public funding of breeds and cultivars whose users keep the right to save seed creates a public alternative to proprietary seed and weakens the incumbent control those companies hold over farmers' planting choices.

The bill keeps the public-private crop insurance system but adds premium discounts for soil-building practices and lets conservation practices qualify as good farming practices, changing underwriting and premiums while the industry retains its role.

A $450,000 five-year cap on EQIP cost-share and tightened CSP payment limits end the ability of the largest operations to absorb outsized shares of conservation dollars, redirecting them to smaller farms.
Composting becomes an eligible conservation practice and new grants fund composting, anaerobic digestion of food waste, and school waste reduction, building a public-supported waste-reduction sector.
The bill expands the Rural Energy for America Program and sets goals to double, then triple, on-farm renewable energy production from 2017 levels.
